Configuring & Integrating MSPs

screens.title: Generating MSP Material: cryptogen vs Fabric CA
screens.narratorSegment: Start by understanding the two supported ways to produce MSP cryptographic material. The cryptogen tool is a utility that reads a crypto-config. yaml topology and produces keys and certificates quickly for every identity you declare. For a two-organization test network this is fast and reproducible: you declare OrdererOrgs and PeerOrgs and cryptogen outputs organized MSP directories. The concrete example you will use in the lab shows a crypto-config. yaml snippet with Orderer and Peer organizations and a single peer host. The important limitation of cryptogen is that it generates private keys for all components centrally and is not designed to simulate a CA, which makes key rotation and real-world identity management harder. In contrast, the Fabric CA client is used in production-like setups. You operate a Fabric CA server, enroll an administrator, and then register and enroll each identity using fabric-ca-client. To assemble an organizational MSP for configtx. yaml you collect only the CA root and intermediate certificates into cacerts and intermediatecerts. This approach avoids putting private keys into the organizational MSP, supports certificate lifecycle operations, and maps well to production security requirements. A common misconception is that cryptogen outputs are production-ready; they are not. Use cryptogen for learning and rapid prototyping, and Fabric CA client for production or when you need revocation and rotation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Generating MSP Material
cryptogen
Quick generation for dev/test
# crypto-config.yaml snippet
OrdererOrgs:
  - Name: Orderer
    Domain: example.com
    Specs:
      - Hostname: orderer
PeerOrgs:
  - Name: Org1
    Domain: org1.example.com
    Template:
      Count: 1
    Users:
      Count: 1
Run: cryptogen generate --config=./crypto-config.yaml to create organizations/ordererOrganizations and organizations/peerOrganizations MSP directories.
Fabric CA client
Production-like enrollment
Start a Fabric CA server, enroll the CA admin, then register and enroll each identity with fabric-ca-client. Collect root and intermediate CA certificates into the organizational MSP's cacerts and intermediatecerts folders.
Example outcome: an organizational MSP containing only public trust roots and a config.yaml that enables NodeOUs.
Use-case: Local dev network
Use-case: Production CA-backed network
Misconception fix: cryptogen is not for production

screens.title: cryptogen: topology to MSP directories
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through using cryptogen to generate MSP directories from a network topology definition. The core idea is simple: crypto-config. yaml declares OrdererOrgs and PeerOrgs and cryptogen produces a mirrored directory structure under organizations. For example, the snippet we use declares Orderer with domain example. com and Org1 with domain org1. example. com. When you run cryptogen generate --config=./crypto-config. yaml, you will find directories such as organizations/ordererOrganizations/example. com/msp and organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp. Each of those MSP directories contains the standard MSP layout — cacerts, tlscacerts, signcerts, keystore, and so on. A concrete example is useful: after running cryptogen on the snippet, verify the presence of cacerts/ca. pem and tlscacerts/tlsca. pem. A common mistake is assuming cryptogen places only public certs into the organizational MSP; it places private keys too, which is why cryptogen output is best for test environments. When preparing an MSP for configtxgen, you should ensure the MSPDir referenced contains only the public trust materials required by configtxgen — in production, assemble a cleaned organizational MSP with public CA roots and config. yaml rather than pointing configtxgen to raw cryptogen output with private keys exposed. Practice checking file permissions and paths; an incorrect MSPDir or missing cacerts will cause configtxgen to fail.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › cryptogen Workflow
Command example
cryptogen generate --config=./crypto-config.yaml
After running, inspect generated paths like organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/msp. Confirm presence of cacerts/ca.pem and tlscacerts/tlsca.pem.
What to check
  • Confirm folder structure: cacerts, tlscacerts, admincerts.
  • Verify file contents: public certs vs private keys.
  • Do not publish private keys included by cryptogen; remove them before creating a production organizational MSP.
Example check: ls organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/msp/cacerts
Common mistake: Pointing MSPDir to a directory that still contains private keystore files.

screens.title: Fabric CA client flow and assembling organizational MSPs
screens.narratorSegment: For production-like networks, the Fabric CA client provides a controlled enrollment process. The typical flow starts by running a Fabric CA server for an organization and enrolling a CA administrator. Using fabric-ca-client you then register identities and enroll them to obtain certificate files for peers, orderers and clients. Crucially, to create an organizational MSP suitable for configtxgen you do not copy private keys into the MSP. Instead you extract the CA public certificates — the root CA and any intermediate CAs — and place those into the cacerts and intermediatecerts directories of a new MSP folder. You then create a config. yaml that enables NodeOUs and maps OU identifiers to the CA certificate path inside the MSP. A concrete example: after enrolling the CA, extract the root certificate file and copy it to organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp/cacerts/ca. pem, and place TLS CA certs into tlscacerts. This assembly makes the organizational MSP a bundle of public trust roots so configtxgen can embed them safely. A common misconception is that each peer's signcerts must be included in the organizational MSP; they must not. The organizational MSP should contain only public trust artifacts and the NodeOU mapping so policies resolve correctly across the channel.

keyIdea.text: Collect only public CA certificates and a config.yaml enabling NodeOUs; do not include private keys or individual identity signcerts in the organizational MSP used by configtxgen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Fabric CA Enrollment
Enrollment steps
  1. Start Fabric CA server for the organization and enroll the CA admin.
  2. Use fabric-ca-client to register and enroll each identity you need.
  3. Extract the CA root and intermediate certs to an organizational MSP folder under cacerts and intermediatecerts.
  4. Create config.yaml enabling NodeOUs that reference the CA cert filename.
Concrete example
Place root cert at organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/msp/cacerts/ca.pem and tls root at tlscacerts/tlsca.pem. Create NodeOUs mapping to cacerts/ca.pem.
Why: supports revocation & rotation
Misconception: do not include private keys in organizational MSP

screens.title: MSP Directory Structure
screens.narratorSegment: An organizational MSP is a predictable directory layout that contains the public trust materials and a NodeOU mapping file. The critical folders are cacerts, intermediatecerts, tlscacerts, admincerts, and a config. yaml. The cacerts folder holds the root CA certificates used to validate signatures for identities issued to peers and clients. tlscacerts holds TLS CA certificates used to validate TLS connections. intermediatecerts is used when your CA issues certificates via an intermediate; include the intermediate chain so other organizations can verify identities. admincerts is sometimes used to explicitly list admin public certificates if you choose that model, though NodeOUs with config. yaml is the recommended approach. The config. yaml controls NodeOU behavior: when enabled, Fabric classifies certificates as client, peer, admin, or orderer based on the OU fields and the referenced CA certificate. A concrete example: a config. yaml with Enable: true and mappings that point each OU to cacerts/ca. pem ensures Fabric recognizes roles in policy evaluation. A common mistake is missing the intermediatecerts file or misnaming the CA pem file so configtxgen cannot locate the trust root. Always verify the directory and file names match what you list in MSPDir.

keyIdea.title: MSP layout
keyIdea.text: cacerts, tlscacerts, intermediatecerts, admincerts, and config.yaml form the organizational MSP needed by configtxgen; names and structure must be exact.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › MSP Directory Structure
Required folders
  • cacerts — root CA public certs for signing identities.
  • tlscacerts — TLS CA certs for TLS verification.
  • intermediatecerts — any intermediate CA certs in the chain.
  • admincerts — optional admin public certs if not using NodeOUs.
  • config.yaml — NodeOU mappings and Enable flag.
Example config.yaml
NodeOUs:
  Enable: true
  ClientOUIdentifier:
    Certificate: cacerts/ca.pem
    OrganizationalUnitIdentifier: client
  PeerOUIdentifier:
    Certificate: cacerts/ca.pem
    OrganizationalUnitIdentifier: peer
Key Takeaway

Exact folder names and correct certificate files are required. Missing or misnamed files break configtxgen and role recognition.

screens.title: Defining Organizations in configtx.yaml
screens.narratorSegment: Configtx. yaml is the canonical place where organizations are defined for configtxgen to consume. Each organization entry includes several important fields. Name is a human readable label. ID is the unique MSP ID used in policies and across the network. MSPDir points to the organizational MSP directory containing cacerts, tlscacerts, and config. yaml. Policies define who can read, write, or administer the organization and often reference roles such as 'Org1MSP. admin' and 'Org1MSP. peer'. AnchorPeers declare the peer endpoints used for inter-organization gossip. A concrete configtx. yaml snippet shows how an Org1 entry might look: Name: Org1MSP, ID: Org1MSP, MSPDir: organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp, followed by Policies and AnchorPeers. When you run configtxgen, it reads MSPDir to embed the public trust roots into the generated genesis. block or channel. tx. A frequent error is an MSPDir that points to the wrong path or an ID mismatch between configtx. yaml and policy references; this will cause configtxgen to fail or channel policies to be evaluated incorrectly at runtime. Always verify MSPDir paths, ensure unique IDs, and include anchor peers for gossip topology.

keyIdea.title: Org definition essentials
keyIdea.text: Name, ID and MSPDir in configtx.yaml tell configtxgen which public trust material to embed and how policies should reference the organization.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › configtx.yaml: Organizations
Example organization entry
Organizations:
    - &Org1
        Name: Org1MSP
        ID: Org1MSP
        MSPDir: organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/msp
        Policies:
            Readers:
                Type: Signature
                Rule: "OR('Org1MSP.admin', 'Org1MSP.peer', 'Org1MSP.client')"
        AnchorPeers:
            - Host: peer0.org1.example.com
              Port: 7051
Fields explained
  • Name: readable label.
  • ID: MSP identifier used in policies.
  • MSPDir: path to organizational MSP with public certs.
Key Takeaway

MSPDir must be accurate and the ID used here must match any policy references. Mismatches cause policy evaluation or artifact generation failures.

screens.title: Policy fields and AnchorPeers
screens.narratorSegment: Policies in configtx. yaml control who can perform actions. Typical policy categories include Readers, Writers, Admins, and Endorsement. Each policy uses a rule that references MSP IDs and roles such as admin, peer, or client, for example OR('Org1MSP. admin'). This means a signature from an identity classified as admin under Org1MSP satisfies the policy. NodeOUs and config. yaml are instrumental because they let Fabric classify certificates into these roles automatically. AnchorPeers are declared under an organization to facilitate cross-organization gossip; they are not about policy but about network discoverability and efficient peer communication. A concrete example: set AnchorPeers for Org1 to point to peer0. org1. example. com:7051 so other orgs can discover Org1 peers. A common misconception is that anchor peers affect endorsement policies — they do not. Anchor peers only affect gossip discovery and channel communication. Always ensure MSP IDs used in policies are spelled exactly as the organization's ID field in configtx. yaml; otherwise policy references will fail at runtime. When debugging policy failures, confirm NodeOU mapping, MSP ID consistency, and that admincerts or NodeOUs are present so the runtime can classify signing identities.

keyIdea.title: Policies & AnchorPeers
keyIdea.text: Policies reference MSP IDs and roles; AnchorPeers enable gossip discovery and do not alter endorsement rules.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Policies & AnchorPeers
Policy example
Policies:
  Readers:
    Type: Signature
    Rule: "OR('Org1MSP.admin', 'Org1MSP.peer', 'Org1MSP.client')"
  Endorsement:
    Type: Signature
    Rule: "OR('Org1MSP.peer')"
Ensure the MSP ID matches the organization ID defined earlier. NodeOUs must be enabled for role-based rules to work automatically.
Anchor peer example
AnchorPeers:
  - Host: peer0.org1.example.com
    Port: 7051
Anchor peers are used for gossip discovery across organizations. They do not change endorsement or access policies.

screens.title: Running configtxgen: producing genesis and channel artifacts
screens.narratorSegment: Once organizations are defined and MSP directories are assembled, configtxgen creates the ordering genesis block and channel creation transactions. The tool reads the Profiles in configtx. yaml and embeds each organization's public MSP data into the generated artifacts. Typical commands include generating a genesis block for the ordering service and creating a channel transaction. For example, to generate a genesis block you might run configtxgen -profile TwoOrgsOrdererGenesis -channelID system-channel -outputBlock./system-genesis-block/genesis. block. To create a channel transaction run configtxgen -profile TwoOrgsChannel -outputCreateChannelTx./channel-artifacts/channel. tx -channelID mychannel. A concrete workflow is: set FABRIC_CFG_PATH to your working directory so configtxgen finds configtx. yaml, ensure all MSPDir paths are correct, then run the commands above. If configtxgen reports it cannot find an MSP, inspect the MSPDir path and the contents of cacerts and config. yaml. A common error arises from missing NodeOU config or misnamed certificate files. After successful generation, the genesis. block informs the ordering service of organization trust roots, and channel. tx carries the channel-level MSPs so peers joining the channel can verify identities. Always verify generated artifacts before starting network components. Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › configtxgen Commands
Generate genesis block
configtxgen -profile TwoOrgsOrdererGenesis -channelID system-channel -outputBlock ./system-genesis-block/genesis.block
Ensure FABRIC_CFG_PATH is set so configtxgen locates configtx.yaml and MSPDirs. Validate that each MSPDir contains cacerts and config.yaml before running.

screens.title: Common MSP Configuration Errors
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting MSP problems is mostly a process of elimination focused on paths, file presence, and NodeOU configuration. The most common error is an incorrect MSPDir path in configtx. yaml. If configtxgen fails saying it cannot find an MSP, first verify that the path is correct relative to FABRIC_CFG_PATH and that the directory contains cacerts and config. yaml. The second common problem is a missing or incorrect config. yaml: when NodeOUs are enabled but the MSP lacks a proper config. yaml mapping, identities will not be recognized as peers, clients or admins and policies will fail. Third, incomplete trust chains cause verification failures — if an intermediate CA issued certificates but you only included the root in cacerts, include intermediatecerts so others can form the full chain. Fourth, MSP ID mismatches — ensure the ID used in policies exactly matches the ID in the organization entry. Finally, avoid using cryptogen artifacts with private keys in organizational MSPDir for production; private keys should not be embedded in organizational MSPs used by configtxgen. A practical diagnosis example: if channel creation fails, check the configtxgen output, verify MSPDir exists, open cacerts and ensure the expected PEM files are present, and inspect config. yaml for NodeOU mappings. Fix the first missing item, then re-run configtxgen.

keyIdea.text: Check MSPDir path, config.yaml for NodeOUs, complete CA chains, MSP ID consistency, and avoid private keys in org MSPs when preparing artifacts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Troubleshooting MSPs
Error: could not find MSP
Fix: verify MSPDir path, ensure directory exists and contains cacerts and config.yaml, check permissions.
Error: role not recognized
Fix: ensure config.yaml exists, NodeOUs enabled, and Certificate paths inside config.yaml point to the correct PEM files.
Error: incomplete trust chain
Fix: include intermediate certificates in intermediatecerts so full chain verification succeeds.
Practical diagnostic steps
  1. Re-run configtxgen and capture the exact error message.
  2. Confirm MSPDir path, file names, and permissions.
  3. Open config.yaml and validate NodeOU mappings.
  4. Check for missing intermediate certs and include them if needed.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: Define Org MSP and generate channel.tx
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through creating a directory structure for an organizational MSP, placing placeholder certificates, building a minimal config. yaml, and running configtxgen to produce a channel transaction. Begin by creating directories under organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp for cacerts, tlscacerts, and admincerts. Add placeholder PEM files to simulate the CA roots. Next, create a config. yaml with NodeOUs enabled and pointing to cacerts/ca. pem. Then, write a configtx. yaml Organizations entry for Org1 using MSPDir: organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp and include basic Policies and an AnchorPeers entry. Set FABRIC_CFG_PATH to your working directory and run configtxgen -profile TwoOrgsChannel -outputCreateChannelTx channel. tx -channelID mychannel. If the command succeeds you have validated that your MSPDir is syntactically correct and that configtxgen can read the public trust roots. If it fails, use the troubleshooting checklist: confirm MSPDir path, file names inside cacerts, NodeOU mapping, and MSP ID matches the organization entry. Reflection prompt: why must MSPDir point to public certs only and not private keys? The short answer is that configtxgen embeds trust roots for verification, and exposing private keys in configuration artifacts compromises identity security.

Shell steps (example)
mkdir -p organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/msp/cacerts
mkdir -p organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/msp/tlscacerts
# create placeholder certs
echo "--- BEGIN CERTIFICATE ---" > organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/msp/cacerts/ca.pem

  • MSPDir exists and contains cacerts and config.yaml.
  • MSP ID in configtx.yaml matches policy references.
  • NodeOUs are enabled and mapped correctly.
  • No private keys are present in the organizational MSP used by configtxgen.
Reflection
Why must the organizational MSP contain only public certs? Because configtxgen embeds trust roots so all parties can verify identities. Including private keys would expose critical secrets and undermine security.

screens.title: Assessment: Integrate an Org MSP into a Three-Org Network
screens.narratorSegment: For assessment, imagine adding OrgA to an existing network with OrgB and OrgC, where each organization runs its own Fabric CA. Next create an organizational MSP directory at organizations/peerOrganizations/orgA. example. com/msp and place the root CA into cacerts and any TLS CA certs into tlscacerts. A common pitfall is forgetting to add OrgA to the Profile that configtxgen uses, which results in artifacts that omit the new organization.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will follow the full path from generating MSP cryptographic material to embedding an organizational MSP into a channel configuration. You will learn two ways to produce MSPs — the quick cryptogen tool and the production-ready Fabric CA client — and why one is suitable for testing and the other for real deployments. We will also examine how configtx. yaml describes an organization with fields such as Name, ID and MSPDir, and how configtxgen turns those definitions into genesis and channel transactions. As we move through the screens you will see concrete file examples, a short terminal demonstration, common errors to avoid, and a small hands-on activity to test your understanding. By the end you should be able to prepare an organizational MSP directory, reference it correctly in configtx. yaml, and run configtxgen to create artifacts that contain your organization’s trust roots. A final reflective question will prompt you to consider how MSPDir content impacts security in production.

Over the next screens you will master four concrete skills essential for configuring MSPs in Hyperledger Fabric. First, you'll be able to define MSP entries inside configtx. yaml and understand why fields such as Name, ID and MSPDir matter. Second, you'll generate MSP cryptographic material using either cryptogen for quick development setups or the Fabric CA client for production-like flows, and you will learn the practical differences between these approaches. Third, you'll integrate generated MSPs into the network by assembling organizational MSP directories and using configtxgen to produce genesis and channel artifacts. Fourth, you'll diagnose and fix common MSP errors such as wrong MSPDir paths, missing NodeOU config, or incomplete trust chains. Each objective will include a short mnemonic or visual cue and a verified competency milestone to help you track progress.

This second objectives screen deepens the practical milestones you'll reach. You will practice organizing MSP directories with the required subfolders and config. yaml so NodeOUs are recognized. You will learn how to extract and place only public CA certificates into cacerts and tlscacerts, and why admincerts belong to administrators while private keys must remain private and never pop into an organizational MSP used by configtxgen. You will also run configtxgen to produce genesis. block and channel. tx, and interpret failures to locate missing files or path errors. Finally, you'll perform a short validation: confirm that the MSP ID used in policies matches the ID in configtx. yaml and that anchor peers are declared for gossip. These skills are aimed at preventing common policy and verification failures during network startup. Learning Objectives — Skills & Troubleshooting means organize msp directories, extract public trust roots correctly, run configtxgen, and validate msp ids and nodeou configuration to avoid runtime policy failures.. In practical terms, practical milestones for secure msp setup. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Start by understanding the two supported ways to produce MSP cryptographic material. The cryptogen tool is a utility that reads a crypto-config. yaml topology and produces keys and certificates quickly for every identity you declare. For a two-organization test network this is fast and reproducible: you declare OrdererOrgs and PeerOrgs and cryptogen outputs organized MSP directories. The concrete example you will use in the lab shows a crypto-config. yaml snippet with Orderer and Peer organizations and a single peer host. The important limitation of cryptogen is that it generates private keys for all components centrally and is not designed to simulate a CA, which makes key rotation and real-world identity management harder. In contrast, the Fabric CA client is used in production-like setups. You operate a Fabric CA server, enroll an administrator, and then register and enroll each identity using fabric-ca-client. To assemble an organizational MSP for configtx. yaml you collect only the CA root and intermediate certificates into cacerts and intermediatecerts. This approach avoids putting private keys into the organizational MSP, supports certificate lifecycle operations, and maps well to production security requirements. A common misconception is that cryptogen outputs are production-ready; they are not. Use cryptogen for learning and rapid prototyping, and Fabric CA client for production or when you need revocation and rotation.

This lesson walks through using cryptogen to generate MSP directories from a network topology definition. The core idea is simple: crypto-config. yaml declares OrdererOrgs and PeerOrgs and cryptogen produces a mirrored directory structure under organizations. For example, the snippet we use declares Orderer with domain example. com and Org1 with domain org1. example. com. When you run cryptogen generate --config=./crypto-config. yaml, you will find directories such as organizations/ordererOrganizations/example. com/msp and organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp. Each of those MSP directories contains the standard MSP layout — cacerts, tlscacerts, signcerts, keystore, and so on. A concrete example is useful: after running cryptogen on the snippet, verify the presence of cacerts/ca. pem and tlscacerts/tlsca. pem. A common mistake is assuming cryptogen places only public certs into the organizational MSP; it places private keys too, which is why cryptogen output is best for test environments. When preparing an MSP for configtxgen, you should ensure the MSPDir referenced contains only the public trust materials required by configtxgen — in production, assemble a cleaned organizational MSP with public CA roots and config. yaml rather than pointing configtxgen to raw cryptogen output with private keys exposed. Practice checking file permissions and paths; an incorrect MSPDir or missing cacerts will cause configtxgen to fail.

For production-like networks, the Fabric CA client provides a controlled enrollment process. The typical flow starts by running a Fabric CA server for an organization and enrolling a CA administrator. Using fabric-ca-client you then register identities and enroll them to obtain certificate files for peers, orderers and clients. Crucially, to create an organizational MSP suitable for configtxgen you do not copy private keys into the MSP. Instead you extract the CA public certificates — the root CA and any intermediate CAs — and place those into the cacerts and intermediatecerts directories of a new MSP folder. You then create a config. yaml that enables NodeOUs and maps OU identifiers to the CA certificate path inside the MSP. A concrete example: after enrolling the CA, extract the root certificate file and copy it to organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp/cacerts/ca. pem, and place TLS CA certs into tlscacerts. This assembly makes the organizational MSP a bundle of public trust roots so configtxgen can embed them safely. A common misconception is that each peer's signcerts must be included in the organizational MSP; they must not. The organizational MSP should contain only public trust artifacts and the NodeOU mapping so policies resolve correctly across the channel.

An organizational MSP is a predictable directory layout that contains the public trust materials and a NodeOU mapping file. The critical folders are cacerts, intermediatecerts, tlscacerts, admincerts, and a config. yaml. The cacerts folder holds the root CA certificates used to validate signatures for identities issued to peers and clients. tlscacerts holds TLS CA certificates used to validate TLS connections. intermediatecerts is used when your CA issues certificates via an intermediate; include the intermediate chain so other organizations can verify identities. admincerts is sometimes used to explicitly list admin public certificates if you choose that model, though NodeOUs with config. yaml is the recommended approach. The config. yaml controls NodeOU behavior: when enabled, Fabric classifies certificates as client, peer, admin, or orderer based on the OU fields and the referenced CA certificate. A concrete example: a config. yaml with Enable: true and mappings that point each OU to cacerts/ca. pem ensures Fabric recognizes roles in policy evaluation. A common mistake is missing the intermediatecerts file or misnaming the CA pem file so configtxgen cannot locate the trust root. Always verify the directory and file names match what you list in MSPDir.

Configtx. yaml is the canonical place where organizations are defined for configtxgen to consume. Each organization entry includes several important fields. Name is a human readable label. ID is the unique MSP ID used in policies and across the network. MSPDir points to the organizational MSP directory containing cacerts, tlscacerts, and config. yaml. Policies define who can read, write, or administer the organization and often reference roles such as 'Org1MSP. admin' and 'Org1MSP. peer'. AnchorPeers declare the peer endpoints used for inter-organization gossip. A concrete configtx. yaml snippet shows how an Org1 entry might look: Name: Org1MSP, ID: Org1MSP, MSPDir: organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp, followed by Policies and AnchorPeers. When you run configtxgen, it reads MSPDir to embed the public trust roots into the generated genesis. block or channel. tx. A frequent error is an MSPDir that points to the wrong path or an ID mismatch between configtx. yaml and policy references; this will cause configtxgen to fail or channel policies to be evaluated incorrectly at runtime. Always verify MSPDir paths, ensure unique IDs, and include anchor peers for gossip topology.

Policies in configtx. yaml control who can perform actions. Typical policy categories include Readers, Writers, Admins, and Endorsement. Each policy uses a rule that references MSP IDs and roles such as admin, peer, or client, for example OR('Org1MSP. admin'). This means a signature from an identity classified as admin under Org1MSP satisfies the policy. NodeOUs and config. yaml are instrumental because they let Fabric classify certificates into these roles automatically. AnchorPeers are declared under an organization to facilitate cross-organization gossip; they are not about policy but about network discoverability and efficient peer communication. A concrete example: set AnchorPeers for Org1 to point to peer0. org1. example. com:7051 so other orgs can discover Org1 peers. A common misconception is that anchor peers affect endorsement policies — they do not. Anchor peers only affect gossip discovery and channel communication. Always ensure MSP IDs used in policies are spelled exactly as the organization's ID field in configtx. yaml; otherwise policy references will fail at runtime. When debugging policy failures, confirm NodeOU mapping, MSP ID consistency, and that admincerts or NodeOUs are present so the runtime can classify signing identities.

Once organizations are defined and MSP directories are assembled, configtxgen creates the ordering genesis block and channel creation transactions. The tool reads the Profiles in configtx. yaml and embeds each organization's public MSP data into the generated artifacts. Typical commands include generating a genesis block for the ordering service and creating a channel transaction. For example, to generate a genesis block you might run configtxgen -profile TwoOrgsOrdererGenesis -channelID system-channel -outputBlock./system-genesis-block/genesis. block. To create a channel transaction run configtxgen -profile TwoOrgsChannel -outputCreateChannelTx./channel-artifacts/channel. tx -channelID mychannel. Troubleshooting MSP problems is mostly a process of elimination focused on paths, file presence, and NodeOU configuration. The most common error is an incorrect MSPDir path in configtx. yaml. If configtxgen fails saying it cannot find an MSP, first verify that the path is correct relative to FABRIC_CFG_PATH and that the directory contains cacerts and config. yaml. Finally, avoid using cryptogen artifacts with private keys in organizational MSPDir for production; private keys should not be embedded in organizational MSPs used by configtxgen.
